Los Angeles.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Los Angeles, CA: You Own the Street Pipe
Los Angeles.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Los Angeles: why you own the lateral to the main, what an S-Permit requires, and why only a bonded contractor can work in the street.
Los Angeles.article:
The half of your lateral you did not know you owned

Most homeowners picture the sewer lateral stopping somewhere near the sidewalk. In Los Angeles it does not. City policy, resting on a City Attorney opinion, places responsibility on the property owner for the house connection lateral from the property line out to the mainline connection, and that includes clearing obstructions caused by tree roots whether those roots are on private ground or in the public right-of-way. The pipe running under the asphalt is your pipe. So is the blockage in it.

That matters before a single quote is read. A bid that covers the yard and stops at the curb has covered part of the asset. If the survey found the defect twenty feet out under the street, the yard portion was never the job.

Why the street portion is a different job

Owning it does not mean you may open it. Under LAMC 64.12 an S-Permit is required to make, construct, alter or repair any house connection sewer, and that covers repairing a damaged lateral as well as connecting to an existing one at the property line. Where the work falls in the public right-of-way, the permit must be obtained by a Bonded Sewer Contractor carrying the appropriate licenses, insurance and bonds, and the Department of Building and Safety inspects and approves the construction.

The practical effect is that the list of firms who may legally work on the street half of your lateral is shorter than the list who may work on the yard half. A plumber perfectly qualified to replace the pipe between the house and the property line may not be able to pull the permit twenty feet further out. Asking about bonded status early is not bureaucratic caution; it decides whether one contractor can finish the job.

What this does to the case for lining

Trenchless work is usually argued on driveways and landscaping. Here the argument is narrower and sharper. Open-cut in the public right-of-way means traffic control, a street cut, compaction to city standard and permanent restoration of the pavement, inspected and signed off. Lining the same length from a pit or an existing cleanout on private ground does not eliminate the permit, but it removes the street cut and everything that follows from it.

That is where the cost difference in Los Angeles actually lives. It is not really the trench. It is the asphalt above the trench and the inspection regime attached to putting it back.

Roots, and the tree that is not yours

Root intrusion is the most common finding in this city and the rule above is worth rereading in that light. The obstruction is the owner's to clear even where the roots came from a tree in the parkway that the owner never planted and may not remove at will. Two conclusions follow. First, an argument about whose tree it is will not change who pays to clear the line. Second, clearing is temporary by definition, because a cutter head removes what is inside the pipe and leaves the opening the roots came through.

A liner is the response to the opening rather than the root. Once the joint is sleeved, there is nothing to enter through along the lined length, which is why a property that has been rodded annually for a decade is usually the strongest candidate for a permanent fix rather than an eleventh visit.

What the age of the housing suggests

Los Angeles has roughly 1.54 million housing units. About 19 percent predate 1940 and about 45 percent predate 1960, with the median unit falling in the 1960s. A city that large contains every vintage at once, so the citywide number is less useful than the block, but it does set expectations. Pre-war construction points to vitrified clay in short jointed lengths with cast iron under the building. The enormous postwar tracts point to clay or cast iron too, and in a narrow window to bituminized fiber conduit, which fails by deforming rather than cracking.

One regional habit is worth naming. Southern California builds on slab far more often than it builds over basements, so the drain line under the house is buried in concrete rather than hanging in an accessible crawlspace. That raises the value of getting the survey right the first time, because verifying a guess is expensive here in a way it is not in a cellar.

What a survey has to establish in this city

Given the boundary, a camera run that stops at the property line has answered the easy half of the question. The footage needs to reach the connection at the main, with a distance counter visible throughout, so the defect can be located against the property line rather than described loosely as being out front. Where the pipe sits relative to that line determines the permit path, the contractor class and the price.

It is also worth establishing the material and the shape separately. A pipe that is cracked but round is a different proposition from one that has lost section, and only the second rules out certain repairs.

Sorting the sequence out first

Before any work is authorized in Los Angeles, three answers change everything that follows: where the defect sits relative to the property line, whether the contractor is bonded for right-of-way work, and who is pulling the S-Permit. A fixed price with exclusions written down is worth more than a lower estimate that turns out to stop at the curb. Closeout should include footage of the finished pipe over its full length and confirmation that any branch connections were reopened.
faq: Does the City of Los Angeles maintain the part of my sewer line under the street?

No. City policy, based on a City Attorney opinion, makes the property owner responsible for the house connection lateral from the property line to the connection at the mainline, including root obstructions in the public right-of-way.
Do I need a permit to repair my sewer lateral?
Yes. LAMC 64.12 requires an S-Permit to make, construct, alter or repair a house connection sewer, which includes repairing a damaged lateral and connecting to an existing one at the property line.
Can any licensed plumber do the work?

Not in the street. Where the work is in the public right-of-way, a Bonded Sewer Contractor must obtain the permit and carry the required licenses, insurance and bonds, and Building and Safety inspects the work. Worth confirming before hiring, since it can split one job between two firms.
The roots came from a city parkway tree. Is the blockage still mine?
Yes. The responsibility for clearing obstructions caused by tree roots sits with the property owner whether the roots are on private property or in the right-of-way.
Why is lining usually cheaper here than replacement?

Because the saving is in the pavement rather than the trench. Open-cut in the right-of-way brings traffic control, a street cut and restoration to city standard, all inspected. Lining from a pit on private ground removes that whole chain.

Long Beach.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Long Beach, CA: One Lateral, Two Diameters
Long Beach.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Long Beach: why your lateral changes from 4 inch to 6 inch at the property line, why you maintain both halves, and what that means for cleaning.
Long Beach.article:
Your lateral is two different pipes

Long Beach Utilities describes the residential sewer lateral in two sections rather than one. From the building out to the sidewalk or property line it is typically four inches, on private ground. From there to the center of the street or alley it is typically six inches, on city ground. The property owner is responsible for routine maintenance of both sections. One asset, two diameters, one owner.

That detail is easy to skim past and hard to ignore once you have seen a camera run. The change in bore is a real physical feature of your line, and it sits precisely at the point where most homeowners assume their responsibility ends.

Why the diameter change is not a technicality

Cleaning equipment is sized to the pipe. A cutter head or nozzle chosen for a four-inch line will pass down the six-inch section without touching much of the wall, which means a line can be rodded, declared clear, and still have roots or scale sitting untouched in the outer half. If a property backs up repeatedly a few weeks after every cleaning, the sizing of the tool against the outer section is worth asking about directly.

For lining, the transition is a design input rather than an obstacle. A liner is specified against the host pipe it has to fit, and a product sized to four inches does not simply expand to fill six. A survey that records where the bore changes, and the length on each side of that point, is doing real work for the quote that follows.

The oldest big-city stock in the region

Of roughly 181,000 housing units in Long Beach, about 19 percent were built before 1940 and about 54 percent before 1960, with the median unit falling in the 1950s and nearly 47 percent built between 1940 and 1969. That is the deepest concentration of genuinely old housing of any large city in Southern California, and it puts most of the city's laterals somewhere between sixty and a hundred years in the ground.

Age narrows the material list to vitrified clay in short jointed lengths, cast iron where the line runs under the structure, and in the postwar stretch a window in which bituminized fiber conduit was used. Those three fail in different directions, which is why a report that names the material is worth more than one that only lists defects.

Damage to the main can come back to you

There is a second clause in the city's position worth noting. Where the actions of a property owner damage or clog the sewer main, the owner can be held responsible for the repairs. That is not an abstract warning. It puts a real cost on decisions that are usually treated as private ones, such as what gets flushed, how grease is handled, and whether a root mass is cut loose and pushed downstream rather than removed.

It also argues for a considered approach to a line that has failed structurally. Fragments of a collapsing pipe do not stay in the lateral.

What lining does with pipe of this vintage

Cured-in-place lining draws a resin-carrying tube through the host pipe and hardens it in position, leaving one unbroken conduit where there were dozens of sockets. In clay it seals every joint along the lined length at once, which is the whole point, because clay's weakness was never the material but the number of openings between lengths. In cast iron it puts an even wall over a floor that has pitted and scalloped away. In fiber conduit the question is different and turns on shape, since a liner cures to whatever cross-section it is pressed against and will not restore a pipe that has gone oval.

The honest limitation is grade. A section that has settled into a dip holds water before lining and holds water afterwards. If the video shows standing water that is not explained by a blockage, that needs answering before a liner is ordered, not after.

Getting a useful survey in a two-section line

Ask for footage that runs the whole way to the connection at the main, with the footage counter running, and ask that the point where the bore changes be called out on the recording. The report should distinguish defects in the four-inch private section from defects in the six-inch section beyond the property line, because the access, the equipment and often the permitting differ between them even though the bill lands in the same place.

Where a cleanout exists, its position relative to the transition matters too. A cleanout that only gives good access to the inner section limits what can be done from it.

Deciding with the whole line in view

The useful discipline in Long Beach is to stop thinking about the lateral as ending at the sidewalk. Price the whole run to the centerline, ask which section each defect sits in, and confirm the tools were sized to both bores. A repair that addresses the four-inch section of a pipe whose problem lies in the six-inch section is not a cheaper fix; it is a postponed one.
faq: Where does my responsibility end in Long Beach?

It does not end at the sidewalk. Long Beach Utilities describes the lateral in two sections, roughly four inches from the building to the property line and six inches from there to the center of the street or alley, and the property owner is responsible for routine maintenance of both.
Why does the pipe change size at the property line?

The private and public-ground sections were built to different standard diameters, typically four inches inside the property line and six inches beyond it. It matters because cleaning tools and liners are sized to the host pipe.
My line keeps backing up a few weeks after cleaning. Why?

One common explanation is that the tool was sized for the four-inch section and passed loosely through the six-inch section without cutting the wall. Asking what diameter the cutter or nozzle was sized for is a fair question.
Can I be charged for damage to the city main?
Yes. Long Beach Utilities states that where the actions of a property owner damage or clog the sewer main, the owner can be held responsible for the repairs.
How old is the typical sewer lateral here?

Old. About 19 percent of the city's housing predates 1940 and about 54 percent predates 1960, with the median unit built in the 1950s, so most laterals have been in the ground between sixty and a hundred years.

Burbank.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Burbank, CA: The City Pays Back Part of It
Burbank.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Burbank: how the SLURP rebates work, why the city pays outright when a parkway tree crushes your lateral, and the order the paperwork demands.
Burbank.article:
Burbank is one of the few cities that pays you back

Most Southern California cities tell a homeowner the lateral is theirs and leave it there. Burbank goes further. Through SLURP, the Sewer Lateral User Rebate Program, the city offers a $150 rebate for cleaning a lateral and a $500 rebate for replacing one, the replacement figure having been set in August 2008. The city also publishes what it expects the work to cost, putting cleaning with a video recording in the $300 to $700 range and installing a cleanout at $300 to $500.

The sums will not fund a project on their own. What they do is reward a homeowner for having the line looked at properly rather than clearing it blind, and that shifts the economics of a first camera run.

The conditions are really a running order

Read the rules as a sequence rather than a list. The cleaning rebate requires a video recording of the cleaned lateral that shows the property address and runs all the way to the connection at the public main. The replacement rebate requires that at least ten feet of the lateral inside the public right-of-way be replaced, and that the contractor obtain permits before work begins. And a property owner is eligible for only one sewer lateral replacement rebate during the life of their ownership.

Each of those decides something before the work starts. Footage that stops short of the main does not qualify. Permits pulled after the fact do not qualify. And because the replacement rebate is once per ownership, it is worth spending on the survey that establishes how much of the line is failing, rather than claiming it on a short patch and discovering the rest of the run six years later.

The parkway tree clause

Separately from the rebates, Burbank will reimburse for damage to a sewer lateral usually maintained by the property owner where the lateral is crushed or displaced by a city-owned tree located in the city-owned parkway. That is a genuinely unusual provision. Across most of the region a homeowner absorbs root damage regardless of whose tree it was.

It puts weight on the survey again, because the claim turns on evidence. Crushed or displaced is a structural finding, visible as deformation or a joint pulled out of line, and it is a different observation from roots having grown in through an open joint. Footage that shows the defect, its distance from the house and its position relative to the parkway is the thing that makes the distinction arguable.

What the housing stock puts under the street

Burbank has about 46,300 housing units. Roughly 53 percent were built before 1960, and just under half were built between 1940 and 1969, with the median unit landing in the 1950s. That is a postwar city with a pre-war core, and the ratio is unusually high for a city of its size in Los Angeles County.

The 1940s and 1960s window matters because it spans the period in which bituminized fiber conduit was installed alongside vitrified clay and cast iron. Clay cracks and admits roots at the joints. Cast iron corrodes from the inside and loses its invert. Fiber conduit does neither and instead deforms until the bore closes, which is why a line of this vintage should be assessed for shape and not only for cracks.

Where responsibility sits, and who to call

The city maintains the mainline; property owners are responsible for maintaining the lateral that connects the building to it. Emergency overflows on private property, or on laterals maintained by the owner, are the owner's responsibility. Emergencies on the city mainline go to Public Works at (818) 238-3915 during business hours and (818) 238-3778 after hours.

Knowing which of those you have is the first diagnostic step, not an administrative afterthought, and it is usually settled by where the water is appearing and whether it correlates with your own usage.

How lining fits the rebate structure

Cured-in-place lining installs a resin-saturated tube that sets hard against the inside wall, closing every socket along the treated run at once and taking away the gaps roots come through. Against clay that is close to the ideal application. Against fiber conduit it depends on whether the pipe has held its round shape, since a liner cures to the cross-section it is pressed against.

Note that the SLURP replacement rebate is written around replacing at least ten feet within the right-of-way. Any homeowner weighing lining against replacement should confirm directly with Public Works how a trenchless rehabilitation is treated before assuming either answer. The rebate is a factor in the decision, not the decision itself.

The order that saves money here

Camera first, with the address on screen and the footage running to the main. Establish material, shape and the location of any defect relative to the parkway. Confirm permits before anyone opens ground. Then decide between lining and replacement with the rebate rules and the once-per-ownership limit in front of you. Done in that order, the paperwork follows the work. Done in any other order, it usually does not.
faq: What is SLURP?

Burbank's Sewer Lateral User Rebate Program. It offers a $150 rebate for cleaning a lateral and a $500 rebate for replacing one, subject to conditions including video documentation and permits pulled in advance.
What does the cleaning rebate require?
A video recording of the cleaned lateral showing the property address and running to the connection at the public sewer main. Footage that stops short of the main does not meet the requirement.
Can I claim the replacement rebate more than once?

No. A property owner is eligible for only one sewer lateral replacement rebate during the life of their ownership of the property, which is a reason to survey the full line before committing to a partial repair.
A city parkway tree crushed my lateral. Who pays?

Burbank states it will reimburse for damage to a lateral otherwise maintained by the property owner where the lateral is crushed or displaced by a city-owned tree in the city-owned parkway. The finding needs to be structural damage rather than root intrusion, so the video evidence matters.
Does lining qualify for the replacement rebate?

The published rule is written around replacing at least ten feet of lateral inside the public right-of-way. Confirm directly with Burbank Public Works how a trenchless rehabilitation is treated before assuming it qualifies.

Pasadena.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Pasadena, CA: Video Before and After
Pasadena.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Pasadena: the city requires pre- and post-lining CCTV, sets a $500 deposit, and restricts pipe bursting. What that means before you hire.
Pasadena.article:
A city that wrote its rules around lining

Most municipal sewer documents were written for digging and mention trenchless work, if at all, as an afterthought. Pasadena's house sewer guidance is not like that. It sets out separate paths for general repair, for relining and for pipe bursting, with different fees and different documentation for each. Whatever else that tells a homeowner, it tells them the city expects these methods to be used and has decided in advance what it wants to see.

That is useful. A published process is one you can plan against, and most of the friction in this kind of project comes from discovering a requirement halfway through.

Where the private pipe actually begins

Pasadena defines the private house sewer as the horizontal piping beginning 24 inches from the exterior wall of the building and extending to its connection with the city sewer line, which is typically at a manhole in the middle of the street. The first two feet out of the wall are not part of it; everything from there to the center of the road is.

The 24-inch mark is worth holding onto, because it is where the plumbing code stops and the sewer permit world starts. A defect inside that distance is a plumbing job. A defect beyond it is a house sewer under this process, with the paperwork that follows.

Video before and video after

For relining, the city requires both a pre-lining and a post-lining CCTV video, submitted to the Public Works permits address. Where no excavation is involved a processing fee applies, with a $500 deposit that is refundable. The specification for the footage is precise: it must run from the nearest private cleanout to the connection with the public sewer main, and it must show the property address, the inspection date and a camera distance read-out continuously throughout.

Those requirements are strict enough that they are worth quoting to a contractor before the first camera goes in the pipe. Footage recorded without the address or the distance counter on screen fails the specification even if it shows the defect clearly, and re-running a survey is an avoidable cost.

There is a quiet benefit for the homeowner in this. A city requiring post-lining video means you finish the job holding independent evidence of what was installed, which is exactly the record that is missing from most sewer repairs a decade later.

The pipe bursting restriction, read as a diagnosis

Pipe bursting is approved case by case, in HDPE or PVC only, with fees equivalent to a new house lateral under the fee schedule and a $500 deposit refundable less the processing fee. The city also states plainly that the method is not suitable for collapsed or blocked pipe.

That last point is more than a permitting rule; it describes the physics. Bursting works by pulling a new pipe along the path of the old one while a head fractures the host outward, and it needs a continuous path to pull through. A pipe that has collapsed no longer offers one. So a survey finding of collapse does not merely rule out one option, it narrows the whole field: lining generally needs a round, continuous host too, and a genuinely collapsed section usually ends in excavation for that length.

What the housing stock suggests is down there

Pasadena has about 62,900 housing units. Close to three in ten went up before 1940, just over half before 1960, and the median unit dates to the 1950s. That is a city with a substantial genuinely pre-war core sitting alongside an equally substantial postwar expansion, and the two carry different expectations.

Pre-1940 construction here usually means vitrified clay, laid in short socketed lengths with a joint at every one, and cast iron on the stretch beneath the house. The postwar half points to clay and cast iron as well, plus the window in which bituminized fiber conduit was installed. Clay admits roots at the joints. Cast iron loses its invert to corrosion. Fiber conduit deforms. The material matters because it determines whether the defect is an opening, a loss of wall, or a loss of shape, and only the third of those reliably defeats a liner.

Pricing the job against the permit path

Because the fee structure differs by method, a quote is more useful in Pasadena when it names the method, the permit path and the deposit separately rather than folding everything into one number. Relining without excavation, relining with a pit, and pipe bursting all sit in different places on the city's schedule, and a homeowner comparing two bids that used different methods is not comparing like for like.

Ask also who submits the videos. It is a small task that is easy for both parties to assume the other is handling, and the deposit refund depends on it.

The order to run this in

Survey first, to the city's specification, from the nearest cleanout to the main with the address, date and counter visible. Establish material, shape and whether any length is collapsed, since that alone decides whether trenchless methods are on the table. Then match the method to the permit path and confirm the deposit and the video submission in writing. Finishing with compliant post-lining footage in hand is worth more than the refund attached to it.
faq: Does Pasadena require video for sewer lining?
Yes, twice. The city requires both a pre-lining and a post-lining CCTV video for relining, submitted to the Public Works permits address, along with a $500 refundable deposit.
What does the video have to show?

It must run from the nearest private cleanout to the connection with the public sewer main, and show the property address, the inspection date and a camera distance read-out continuously. Footage missing any of those does not meet the specification.
Where does my house sewer start?

Pasadena defines the private house sewer as the horizontal piping beginning 24 inches from the exterior wall of the building and running to its connection with the city sewer line, usually at a manhole in the middle of the street.
Can I use pipe bursting in Pasadena?
Case by case, in HDPE or PVC only, with fees equivalent to a new house lateral and a $500 deposit refundable less the processing fee. The city notes it is not suitable for collapsed or blocked pipe.
My camera survey found a collapsed section. What does that rule out?

Bursting needs a continuous path to pull a new pipe along, and lining needs a round, continuous host to cure against. A genuinely collapsed length usually has to be excavated, even where the rest of the run can be lined.

Glendale.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Glendale, CA: Yours to the Middle of the Street
Glendale.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Glendale: the city says you own the pipe to the center of the street including the connection, and asks to inspect while the trench is open.
Glendale.article:
The city states it without hedging

Municipal websites tend to describe sewer responsibility in careful, lawyerly language. Glendale does not bother. Its Public Works FAQ tells residents that they own the waste pipe all the way up to the city's main line under the middle of the street, including the connection at the main. No boundary at the sidewalk, no shared section, no ambiguity about the tap itself.

Including the connection is the part most homeowners have never considered. The saddle or wye where your lateral meets the city main is an item that can fail on its own, independently of the pipe leading to it, and in Glendale it is squarely yours.

What that adds to the length you are pricing

A typical residential lot puts the building some distance back from the property line, and the property line some distance back from the center of the road. The stretch beyond the sidewalk is frequently a third or more of the total run, and it is the stretch under pavement. Any quote should therefore be read against a stated length to the main rather than a length to the property line.

It also changes how a repeated blockage should be interpreted. If a line is cleared from a cleanout near the house and the problem returns, the question is not only what was found but how far the equipment actually reached. A tool that stopped short of the connection has not surveyed the part of the pipe you own furthest from the house and are least likely to have ever seen.

The open-trench window

Glendale asks to be called to inspect the lateral while it is exposed, through Maintenance Services at (818) 548-3950. That request is easy to read as a formality and is worth treating as an opportunity instead.

An open trench is the only moment when the pipe can be examined directly rather than through a camera lens, and it is a short window: excavations get backfilled the same day more often than not. Making the call before the hole is closed costs nothing and produces a city record of the condition of the line and of the work performed. If a dispute about the connection or the right-of-way ever arises, that record is the difference between an account and an assertion.

What is likely to be in the ground

Glendale has about 78,500 housing units. Roughly 21 percent were built before 1940 and about 43 percent before 1960, with the median unit in the 1960s. That is a city with a solid pre-war core and a larger postwar body, and the spread means the block matters more than the citywide figure.

The older stock points to segmented clay on the outdoor run and cast iron beneath the building. The postwar stock points to clay and cast iron again, and to the period in which bituminized fiber conduit saw use. These fail along different axes. Clay stays chemically sound and opens at the joints. Cast iron corrodes inward and loses the bottom of the bore first. Fiber conduit keeps its wall and loses its shape. A camera report that names the material is doing more for the decision than one that only lists cracks and roots.

What lining does across that length

Lining works by pulling a resin-bearing tube through the old pipe and curing it hard where it sits. Over a long run to the middle of the street its chief advantage is that it treats every joint in one pass, which suits clay precisely, since clay's problem is the number of openings rather than the strength of the material. It also seals the line against groundwater moving in and sewage moving out along the lined length.

Two limits are worth stating plainly. A liner takes the shape of the host pipe, so a section that has gone oval or settled into a dip will still be oval or still hold water afterwards. And the connection at the main, now known to be yours, is a detail to ask about specifically, since how a liner is terminated there is a design question rather than an assumption.

Getting the survey to cover what you own

Ask for footage that runs to the connection at the main, with the footage count on screen, and ask what was found at the tap itself rather than only along the run. Ask whether the camera was stopped by something or reached the end. A survey that terminated early because of a bend or a root mass should be described that way, not summarized as the line being clear to that point.

Where access is limited, a cleanout installed in the right position is usually a good investment before anything else, because it makes every future inspection cheaper and every future cleaning more effective.

Deciding what is worth doing

The Glendale rule is clarifying rather than discouraging. Knowing the whole run is yours removes the most common source of wasted money in this work, which is paying to investigate or repair on the assumption that someone else owns the other end. Price the full length, survey the full length, call the city while the ground is open, and keep the record.
faq: Where does my sewer responsibility end in Glendale?
At the main. The city's Public Works FAQ states that you own the waste pipe all the way up to the city's main line under the middle of the street, including the connection at the main.
Does that include the connection at the city main?
Yes. Glendale names the connection explicitly, which matters because the saddle or wye can fail on its own independently of the pipe leading to it.
Should I call the city when my lateral is dug up?

Yes. Glendale asks to be called to inspect the lateral while it is exposed, through Maintenance Services at (818) 548-3950. It is a short window, since trenches are usually backfilled quickly, and it produces a city record of the condition and the work.
How much extra pipe is beyond the sidewalk?

On a typical lot the stretch from the property line to the center of the road is often a third or more of the total run, and it is the part under pavement. Quotes should state the length to the main, not to the property line.
Will lining fix a sagging section?

No. A liner cures to the shape of the pipe it is pressed against, so a section that has settled into a dip will still hold water afterwards. Standing water on the video needs explaining before a liner is ordered.

Beverly Hills.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Beverly Hills, CA: The Code Lists Your Chores
Beverly Hills.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Beverly Hills: BHMC 6-1-307 names periodic inspection, jetting and root treatment as owner duties. What that implies for an older lateral.
Beverly Hills.article:
An ordinance that describes maintenance, not just ownership

Nearly every city in the region says who owns the sewer lateral. Beverly Hills goes a step further and says what the owner is expected to be doing with it. Under BHMC 6-1-307, maintenance and repair of the private drainage system and all of its component parts is the sole responsibility of the property owner, covering building sewers and private sewer laterals up to the point of connection with the public sewer.

Then the code names the work: periodic inspection of all components of the drainage system, and repair, cleaning, flushing, hydro-jetting, snaking or treatment for the removal of roots and fats, oils and grease as needed. Few municipal codes are that specific about a homeowner's routine, and the specificity is the point.

Periodic inspection as a written expectation

Most owners treat a sewer camera as something you pay for after a backup. Here, periodic inspection is named in the ordinance as part of ordinary upkeep. Read that way, a survey is closer to servicing a boiler than to calling a plumber in an emergency, and the difference in timing changes what the survey can be used for.

A line inspected while it is still working gives you options: monitor, clean, line a section, plan. A line inspected during a backup gives you one option, chosen under pressure, usually at a premium, and frequently without time to compare methods or contractors.

Older stock than the reputation suggests

Beverly Hills has about 16,500 housing units, and nearly a third of them went up before 1940. Just over half predate 1960, and the median unit dates to the 1950s. Nearly a third of the city predating the Second World War is a higher share than most of Los Angeles County, and it puts a great many laterals close to or past ninety years old.

Pipe of that age is almost always clay — segmented, socketed and perfectly sound in itself — with cast iron on the length beneath the house. Clay does not decay, which is precisely the trap: the material can be sound while the line is failing, because clay's vulnerability is the joint count rather than the wall. Cast iron is the opposite and degrades from the inside, thinning along the invert until it perforates.

The postwar half of the city adds the window in which bituminized fiber conduit was used. It fails by losing shape rather than by cracking, which is why an inspection should report the roundness of the bore and not only the presence of defects.

Roots and grease, named in the code for a reason

The two things the ordinance singles out for treatment are the two things that actually close residential sewer lines. Roots enter through openings and grow into the flow; they do not drill through sound pipe. Fats, oils and grease cool, congeal and accumulate on any rough or irregular surface, which is why they collect at corroded cast iron and at displaced joints rather than uniformly along the run.

Both are therefore symptoms of a surface condition as much as habits. A line that needs rodding every year is telling you something about its interior, and the recurrence interval is often more diagnostic than the blockage itself.

Backwater valves and the other appurtenances

The code lists backwater valves, clarifiers, ejectors, grease traps and interceptors among the owner-maintained components. It requires that they be maintained where they exist rather than mandating that they be installed, which is a distinction worth understanding before a contractor offers one as a solution.

A backwater valve protects against flow coming back toward the house from the public system. It does nothing about a root mass or a broken pipe between the house and the main, and it is not an alternative to repairing the line. Where one is fitted, it is a moving part in a sewer and needs to be checked, which is precisely why the code names it.

What lining addresses in a line of this age

Cured-in-place lining leaves a seamless tube bonded against the inside of the original, closing the sockets along the treated run in one operation. Against ninety-year-old clay that is a direct answer to the actual failure mode, since it removes every opening at once rather than repairing them one at a time. Against corroded cast iron it restores a smooth bore, which also reduces the surface that grease adheres to.

The limits are the usual honest ones. A liner does not correct grade, does not restore a collapsed or badly deformed section, and does not reach anything the survey did not cover. Those constraints argue for the inspection the ordinance already asks for.

Treating it as scheduled work

The practical reading of BHMC 6-1-307 is that a sewer lateral here is an asset with a maintenance schedule rather than a fixture that gets attention when it fails. For most properties in this city that means a camera survey on a sensible interval, cleaning that removes material rather than merely opening a channel through it, and a decision about lining made from a video rather than from a flooded floor.
faq: Who is responsible for the sewer lateral in Beverly Hills?

The property owner. BHMC 6-1-307 provides that maintenance and repair of the private drainage system and all of its component parts is the sole responsibility of the property owner, up to the point of connection with the public sewer.
Does the city code actually require inspections?

The ordinance names periodic inspection of all components of the drainage system among the owner's maintenance obligations, alongside cleaning, flushing, hydro-jetting, snaking and treatment for roots and grease.
Am I required to install a backwater valve?

The code lists backwater valves among owner-maintained appurtenances and requires they be maintained where present. It does not mandate installation. A valve also does not substitute for repairing a failed lateral.
How old is the typical lateral here?
About 30 percent of the city's housing was built before 1940 and about 51 percent before 1960, with the median unit in the 1950s, so many laterals are close to or beyond ninety years in the ground.
My line needs rodding every year. Is that normal?

It is common but it is not a maintenance schedule, it is a symptom. Roots enter through openings and grease collects on rough or irregular surfaces, so an annual recurrence usually points to a surface condition that clearing does not change.

Culver City.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Culver City, CA: Who May Dig in the Street
Culver City.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Culver City: the code limits street excavation to four license classes, and half the city's housing went up between 1940 and 1969.
Culver City.article:
The permit rule that shapes the hiring decision

Culver City Municipal Code 5.02.225 requires a permit before making, constructing, altering or repairing a house connection sewer, or any portion of such a connection. Clearing a stoppage generally does not need one, unless the work requires replacement or excavation in a street or easement. So the permit question turns less on the severity of the problem than on whether anyone is going to open ground in public space.

That threshold is worth knowing before you compare bids, because it is the point at which two quotes for the same symptom stop being comparable. Rodding a line and replacing a length of it under the road are different undertakings under this code, whatever the backup looked like in the kitchen.

Four license classes, and why the distinction matters

The code is specific about who may excavate in a public street: city departments, other governmental agencies, or contractors holding a California A-1 general engineering, B-1 general building, C-36 plumbing or C-42 sewer and sewage disposal license. A permit for making sewer connections at the property line may be issued to any responsible person where the Director determines it will not endanger public property.

Two different standards, then, for two parts of the same job. A firm entirely capable of the work inside the property line may not hold a classification that lets it excavate beyond it. Asking which classification a contractor holds is a short question that prevents the common and expensive outcome of a project stopping at the curb line and a second firm being brought in to finish it.

Of the four, C-42 is the classification written specifically for sewer and sewage disposal work, and A-1 covers general engineering. Either is a reasonable thing to see on a bid for work in the roadway.

A postwar city, not an old one

Culver City's housing profile is distinctive. Of about 19,100 units, only around 11 percent predate 1940, but roughly 48 percent predate 1960 and nearly 51 percent were built between 1940 and 1969 — the highest concentration of that single period anywhere in this group of cities. The median unit sits in the 1960s.

That means Culver City's sewer problem is not primarily a pre-war clay problem. It is a mid-century problem, and the mid-century used a wider palette. Vitrified clay was still being laid. Cast iron ran under buildings. And the 1940s through 1960s is the window in which bituminized fiber conduit, a bitumen-impregnated wood fiber pipe, went into residential laterals in quantity.

Why the material changes the survey brief

Those three materials fail in different directions and reward different questions. Clay stays chemically intact and opens at the joints, so the useful finding is how many joints are displaced or rooted. Cast iron corrodes inward, thinning along the bottom of the bore, so the useful finding is how much wall remains. Fiber conduit keeps its wall and loses its cross-section, so the useful finding is whether the pipe is still round.

Only the third of those is routinely missed. A camera operator looking for cracks and roots can pass through an ovalled fiber line and report it as intact, because there is nothing broken to see. An inspection in a city of this vintage should be asked specifically to comment on the shape of the bore.

Slab construction and the cost of a second look

Mid-century Southern California built on slab far more often than over basements, which means the drain line under the house sits in concrete rather than in an accessible crawlspace. There is no cellar to walk into and confirm a suspicion.

The practical consequence is that guesses are expensive to check here. It is worth paying once for a survey that reaches the main, records distances and names materials, rather than paying twice because the first inspection was scoped only to find the immediate blockage.

What lining does with mid-century pipe

Lining turns a jointed run into a single unbroken conduit without taking the old pipe out of the ground. In clay it closes every joint along the lined length in a single pass, which is the most direct possible answer to a joint-count problem. In cast iron it replaces a pitted, scalloped floor with an even surface, which incidentally gives grease far less to cling to.

In fiber conduit the answer depends entirely on shape, and this is the honest limit. A liner cures against the host pipe and takes its form, so a round fiber line can be lined and an ovalled one cannot be restored by lining. That is one reason the survey question above is not academic.

Getting the scope right before the permit

Establish first whether any part of the proposed work falls in the street or an easement, because that determines the permit and the eligible contractor classes. Ask for footage that runs to the main with distances logged throughout, and ask for the material and the roundness of the bore to be reported separately from the defects. Then price the job as a whole rather than as the portion inside the property line. A bid that ends where the permitting begins has quoted the easy part.

Who is allowed to excavate in the street?

City departments, governmental agencies, or contractors holding a California A-1 general engineering, B-1 general building, C-36 plumbing or C-42 sewer and sewage disposal license. Connections at the property line may be permitted to any responsible person at the Director's determination.
Why does the license classification matter to me?

Because a firm able to work inside your property line may not hold a classification that allows excavation beyond it. Asking early avoids a project stopping at the curb and a second contractor being needed to finish.
What kind of pipe is likely under a Culver City house?

Roughly 51 percent of the city's housing was built between 1940 and 1969, so mid-century materials dominate: vitrified clay, cast iron under the building, and bituminized fiber conduit from the window in which it was installed.
Can a camera miss a failing fiber conduit pipe?

It can. Fiber conduit fails by losing its round shape rather than by cracking, so an operator looking for breaks and roots may pass through and report the line intact. Ask specifically for a comment on the roundness of the bore.

Arcadia.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Arcadia, CA: The Mains Get Cleaned, Yours Does Not
Arcadia.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Arcadia: the city jets 135 miles of main on an 18-month rotation and states plainly it does not own or maintain private sewer laterals.
Arcadia.article:
Two systems, one schedule between them

Arcadia's Sewer System Management Plan describes an organized preventative program on the public side. The city maintains about 135 miles of gravity sewer, cleaned on an eighteen-month rotation with high-velocity jetter trucks, and priority areas are cleaned every 30, 90 or 180 days where there is a history of blockages, overflows, or CCTV analysis suggesting it. Inverted siphons get particular attention because grease and settled debris accumulate there.

The same document is equally clear about the other half. The Public Works Services Department does not own or maintain sewer laterals from private properties connected to the sewer main. So the pipe in the street is on a schedule; the pipe from your house to it is on whatever schedule you give it.

The asymmetry is the practical point

It is easy to assume that a sewer system that visibly functions is being looked after end to end. In most cities, including this one, it is not. The public main benefits from routine jetting and a CCTV-informed priority list. The private lateral, which is usually older than any recent main work and always narrower, receives attention only when a homeowner arranges it.

Narrower matters more than people expect. A four-inch lateral tolerates far less root mass or grease before it closes than a main does, and it has more joints per foot of run. The part of the system least likely to be inspected is the part most likely to fail.

An almost entirely postwar city

Arcadia's housing profile is unusual and useful. Of roughly 20,900 units, only about 4 percent were built before 1940 — a very small pre-war share — yet about 43 percent predate 1960, and nearly 55 percent of the whole city went up in the thirty years after the war. The median unit falls in the 1960s.

That combination is rare. It means this is not a city where the sewer conversation is about ninety-year-old clay. It is a city built almost entirely inside a thirty-year window, so the laterals are unusually consistent in age, and a finding on one block is a reasonable working hypothesis for the next.

What that window put in the ground

The 1940s through the 1960s laid clay out to the street, cast iron beneath the house, and — where it was available and cheap — bituminized fiber conduit. The three materials are genuinely different problems.

Clay is chemically stable and fails by opening at the joints, admitting roots and groundwater. Cast iron corrodes from the inside and loses the bottom of the bore before it perforates. Fiber conduit does not crack and does not corrode; it deforms, gradually flattening until the bore closes. A survey that reports only cracks and roots has no vocabulary for the third of those, which is why the roundness of the pipe should be reported explicitly.

Reading your own symptoms against the city's program

Knowing that mains are jetted on a rotation, and that problem areas are on much shorter cycles, gives a homeowner a useful reference point. A property that backs up repeatedly while the public system in the street is on a routine schedule is describing a private-side problem, and treating it as a city issue will only delay the diagnosis.

The inverse is worth noting too. If several neighbours are experiencing the same thing at the same time, that pattern points outward rather than inward, and is worth reporting rather than each household independently paying to rod its own line.

What lining changes for a line of this vintage

The lining process cures a resin-impregnated tube hard against the inside wall, producing one uninterrupted pipe where there had been dozens of sockets. Against clay laid in short jointed lengths in the 1950s and 1960s, that addresses the thing that actually went wrong: the problem was never the strength of the clay, it was how many openings there were between the house and the street.

The limits are worth stating as clearly as the benefits. A liner cures to the shape of the host, so it does not restore an ovalled fiber line and does not correct a section that has settled into a dip. It does not repair a collapse. And it only covers what was surveyed, which is the argument for a camera run that goes the full distance rather than to the first defect.

Putting your half on a schedule

The sensible response to the asymmetry is to give the private side a cycle of its own rather than waiting for a symptom. A survey to the main with distances recorded and materials named gives you a baseline. A cleaning that removes material rather than boring a channel through it buys real time. And a decision about lining made from video, on a schedule of your choosing, is almost always cheaper than the same decision made on the day the line closes.

No. The city's Sewer System Management Plan states that the Public Works Services Department does not own or maintain sewer laterals from private properties that are connected to the sewer main.
How often does the city clean its sewer mains?

About 135 miles of gravity sewer is cleaned on an eighteen-month rotation using high-velocity jetter trucks, with priority areas on 30, 90 or 180 day cycles based on blockage and overflow history or CCTV analysis.
If the mains are cleaned regularly, why does my line back up?

Because your lateral is not part of that program and is both older and narrower than the main. A four-inch lateral closes on far less root mass or grease than a main does, and it has more joints per foot.
What era is most Arcadia housing from?
Almost entirely postwar. Only about 4 percent predates 1940, while roughly 55 percent was built between 1940 and 1969, with the median unit in the 1960s.
Several neighbours have the same problem at once. What does that suggest?
A shared cause in the public system rather than a private-side defect. That pattern is worth reporting to the city rather than each household separately paying to clear its own lateral.

Laguna Beach.metaTitle: CIPP Lining in Laguna Beach, CA: A Remodel Can Trigger It
Laguna Beach.metaDescription: CIPP lining in Laguna Beach: chapter 17.50 requires cleaning, video and a report after a spill, a remodel over $100,000, or a change of use. 90 days to fix.
Laguna Beach.article:
The city with an actual lateral ordinance

Southern California is, on the whole, a region without private sewer lateral ordinances. The compliance program that certify laterals before a property changes hands cluster in the Bay Area. Laguna Beach is the local exception, and it is worth understanding because the obligations are real and the triggers are not the ones most owners expect.

Under LBMC 17.50.040, owners must maintain private sewer laterals up to and including the connection to the public sewer, which the code says may include periodic video inspection, cleaning, repair and replacement. It goes on to require that owners maintain, inspect, repair or replace as needed to prevent sanitary sewer overflows. The duty is framed around an outcome, not a checklist.

What actually triggers an inspection

LBMC 17.50.052 sets out the events that require cleaning, video inspection and an inspection report. A spill from the private lateral is one. So is a remodel involving bathroom, kitchen or laundry work, or any project exceeding $100,000. So is a change of use from residential to commercial, or a property standing vacant for more than three years. Repair or replacement of any portion of the lateral triggers it, as does major work on the main the lateral connects to, or a city notice that the lateral is not functioning adequately.

Note what is not on that list: sale of the property. This is not a point-of-sale ordinance and should not be described as one. It is a trigger-based program, and the trigger most likely to catch a homeowner unprepared is the remodel one, because a kitchen or bathroom project is planned months in advance around a budget that rarely includes a sewer survey.

Ninety days, running from the earliest date

Where corrective work is required, LBMC 17.50.040(g) sets a correction grace period of 90 days, running from the earliest of the notice being issued, the inspection date, or the testing date. The detail that matters is earliest. The clock can already have been running for weeks by the time a notice arrives, if the inspection preceded it.

Ninety days is a workable window for a lined lateral and a tight one for a project requiring excavation, permits and restoration in a city with the street geometry Laguna has. That asymmetry is a real argument for establishing the condition of the line before a remodel is designed rather than after it is underway.

What the certificate requires

LBMC 17.50.060 provides for a certificate of compliance where the lateral is free of roots, grease and non-sanitary connections, and has sound joints, structural integrity, and proper cleanouts and backflow protection. That is a more complete definition of a passing lateral than most homeowners have ever been given, and it repays reading as a specification rather than as legal text.

Two items on it are commonly missing rather than defective. Non-sanitary connections — a downspout or an area drain tied into the sanitary lateral — are a legacy of older properties and do not show up as a fault in normal use. And a proper cleanout is often simply absent on an older house, which is an installation rather than a repair. Both are worth identifying at the survey stage, because neither is discovered by waiting.

The housing behind the requirement

Laguna Beach has about 13,600 housing units. Roughly 16 percent were built before 1940 and about 43 percent before 1960, with nearly 47 percent built between 1940 and 1969 and the median unit in the 1960s. It is an older coastal city with a substantial mid-century body.

That points to segmented clay on the outside run, cast iron beneath the building, and fiber conduit in the postwar window. It also points to a practical local complication: hillside lots and narrow, steep streets make excavation genuinely difficult here in a way it is not on a flat grid, which changes the arithmetic between lining and replacement before any other factor is considered.

Why lining suits the ordinance well

Lining sets a seamless tube against the inside face of the host pipe, closing every socket along the treated run at once. Read against the certificate criteria, that addresses several items in one operation: it removes the openings roots enter through, it restores structural continuity along the lined length, and it seals the joints that let groundwater in and sewage out — which is precisely the overflow prevention the ordinance is aimed at.

It does not do everything. It will not correct a sagging section, restore a collapsed or ovalled length, disconnect a non-sanitary connection, or install a cleanout where none exists. Those are separate line items, and a quote that is being written against a compliance certificate should name them separately.

Getting ahead of the trigger

The efficient move in Laguna Beach is to survey the lateral while nothing is compelling you to. A remodel is the most common trigger and the most predictable one, which makes it the easiest to plan around. Knowing the condition of the line before the architect finishes turns a 90-day compliance problem into a scheduling decision, and usually into a cheaper one.
faq: Does Laguna Beach require a sewer lateral inspection when I sell?

No. Chapter 17.50 is trigger-based rather than sale-based. The triggers include a spill from the lateral, a remodel involving bathroom, kitchen or laundry work or exceeding $100,000, a change of use, a vacancy of more than three years, repair or replacement of any part of the lateral, major work on the connecting main, or a city notice.
My remodel is over $100,000. What does that mean for my sewer?

LBMC 17.50.052 requires cleaning, video inspection and an inspection report. It is worth surveying the lateral before the project is designed, so any corrective work can be folded into the schedule rather than added to it.
How long do I have to fix a problem?

LBMC 17.50.040(g) allows a 90 day correction grace period, running from the earliest of the notice issuance, the inspection date or the testing date. Because it runs from the earliest date, the clock may already have started before a notice arrives.
What does a lateral need to pass?

Under LBMC 17.50.060 the certificate of compliance requires the lateral to be free of roots, grease and non-sanitary connections, with sound joints, structural integrity, and proper cleanouts and backflow protection.
What is a non-sanitary connection?

Something like a downspout or an area drain tied into the sanitary lateral. It is common on older properties, causes no symptom in normal use, and is named in the compliance criteria, so it is worth identifying during the survey rather than at the certificate stage.
